After 117 hours of wasting my time as a 17 year old high schooler to maintain a promise I made when I was seven to 100% any Lego game I played. I finally did it today. This game literally took me back in time to where I was playing The Complete Saga on the DS and the Wii. It was a much needed "one last time" event that took me back before I become a legal adult. And although I can never go back in time, this game certainly did just that... except for the fact that its not a DS that I could take with me where ever I wanted or a Wii that that kept crashing every few weeks.

Let me start out by saying two things. 1: I like the Complete Saga better, but that may be because that game was my childhood. 2: This is a fantastic successor to the CS. Now I will get into what I view as the pros and cons of the game. SPOILERS?

Pros: 
1. Lego humor has never been funnier
2. The game is open world
3. Ship combat is fun
4. The visuals are stunning 
5. There is so much to do
6. Taking a capital ship is fun
7. There are so many details in this game
8. Can't believe I have to say this but in today's gaming industry we finally have a game that isn't a mess at launch 
9. Side quests are fun 

Cons: 
1. My biggest gripe is that when it comes to the actual missions they feel lacking in content, they could have added more from each episode for sure. My biggest issue with this is that there is no level for the opening battle scene from Revenge of the Sith, that was my favorite level in Complete Saga. That may just be me though 
2. This isn't really a con for me because I am definatly a more casual gamer, and this is a game for children, but the game is very easy. If your tired of Dark Souls and Elden Ring and just want to relax look no further. 

This game is for sure worth the 2 year delay and the $60

This game is great not just for the men, but the women and the children as well

Skywalker Saga... Tt Games' most ambitious Lego game to date. I was hyped for this game. I was hyped since it was first announced. All nine mainline films in one package, enhanced with a new game engine, graphics, overhauled gameplay and combat... I was interested. Intrigued. This was the first game i ever pre-ordered, shelled out a couple extra for deluxe edition. Was my hype met now that i've finally played it? Some of it was elevated... Some of it met the limit of my hype... But most of this game... It fell below that hype. 

I'll start with my positives. This game is absolutely GORGEOUS. It is a feast for the eyes anywhere you go. This is Tt Games' art and environment teams let absolutely loose and they delivered in droves. With the 24 planets that can be explored with the little areas within them, both teams captured the look of these planets and Star Wars perfectly. The detail of sand or snow covering parts of your characters the more they run around the sands of Tatooine, Pasana, Jakku or the snows of Hoth add to the detail put into this game.

The humor in cutscenes is also top notch, probably the funniest i've watched to date. Remember that i'm exclusively flagging the word "cutscenes". 

The fights versus Capital Ships were fun? Sometimes fighting the boss of the ship was a bit off.

The negatives... This game otherwise feels... Soulless. Let me explain.

The movies, for lack of a better word, are "cannibalised" to me. To make an example, let's start where i did. Episode 1. Now the first level of Phantom Menace in Complete Saga should be nostalgic to anyone. Might take up of 4-5 minutes to complete, utilises the Force skills of the two Jedi and shows how to use protocol droids to open certain panels. Skywalker Saga? You can hold down sprint, ignore every enemy in your way and be done this story section in a minute or two. Negotiations isn't even Phantom Menace's first proper level. It's just a point A to B run. Followed by more point A to B running tagging along with Jar Jar to go towards the Gungan city of Otoh Gunga... Where you do more walking to get to another cutscene AND THEN the first level begins... The underwater submarine trip to Theed, dodging the fish trying to eat the heroes. 

Each movie is just rushed through to get to a short level where you can basically use one character to get through it all. Either that or an incredibly short vehicle level. There's no real puzzles to Skywalker Saga's levels when compared to other Lego or Lego Star Wars games. I made an example of Complete Saga's "Negotiations" level and how you use two character types to beat it. Encouraging swapping characters in solo play or cooperative play. Skywalker Saga just feels like a nothing burger in between running from cutscene to cutscene to level.

Character uniqueness is robbed with the introduction of the class/skill system. To take from the Force Awakens game, Finn can use First Order terminals right through the game. Even when he joins the Resistance, he can still use them. Because that's in his character as a former First Order soldier. Here? The moment he swaps from the "Evil" class to the "Hero" class, he loses ALL access to "Evil" class terminals which he can use in the first level of Skywalker Saga's Force Awakens level. 

My least favorite addition to levels in this game have to be the tied in "Challenges". Unless you buy the rumor to get a vague hint at what to do or look online, these challenges will remain locked behind random question marks. Extra faff on top of a new three tier True Jedi stud bar (Why three? We've had the one "True" stud bar for over a decade and it makes no sense) and five minikits to dig up. Just chop out the challenges and turn every level from 6 Kyber Bricks to 5. 

The vehicles themselves often times decided to not work with me when i turned. Like sometimes the vehicle would "stick" in one direction for a few seconds and would only fix if i kept aggressively swiping my mouse where i wanted to turn. This basically killed all vehicle levels and space sections most of the time. Thankfully these levels are painfully short so i could get back into the mindless point A-B cutscene to cutscene running.

So what about the open worlds i hear you ask? With 24 planets to go to, surely there's something there other than their looks?

And you'd be wrong. I streamed my 100% Kyber Brick and Side Mission grind on Discord to my girlfriend. And even she could pick up how bored i must have been immediately picking up a Kyber Brick after a "puzzle" that wouldn't even require someone to rub two braincells together, opening the holomap, clicking on the next Brick rumor and immediately sprinting towards it to rinse and repeat until i was done. And she was right.

There are 1200 Kyber Bricks in Skywalker Saga. Where the recent Lego games had over 200 Gold Bricks to chase down, any found in the open world at least required a degree of thinking. In simple terms, Skywalker Saga took quantity over quality. So i hope you're in for an incredibly boring grind to a 100% save file. I hope you find the stud fountain worth it... Or the completely patronising clapping from the main heroes of the trilogies. 1200 Kyber Bricks later and that's it? 

Speaking of quantity over quality, i sure hope you enjoy the copy and paste puzzles found on every planet let alone the capital ships... Those are the most egregious when it comes to the rule. Because all nine capital ships share the EXACT SAME KYBER BRICK "PUZZLES". Maybe one variation between each of them but that's just me being generous. The side missions themselves can often be drawn out too if the quest tasks you with going off world to a different planet or three. And don't get me started on ANY mission requiring you to smuggle goods from one planet to another. Because every time you take one of those quests, you get three waves of space combat that pulls you out of hyperspace before you get to your destination. And given how dumb the enemies are, it's just a matter of pursuing them to line up shots. Tedium in a nutshell. 

I've even encountered enemies in the side quests or the bosses of the Capital Ship raids that for an extended period of time would just refuse to take damage after shooting them and then miraculously they took a bolt and became invulnerable again. This became even more laughable once i upgraded the Bounty Hunter class with the amount of bolts they can burst fire and kept on shooting some quest essential enemies or Capital Ship bosses. It didn't matter how many ridiculous spray and pray bolts hit my target, the game made them immortal until it said otherwise, turned off the switch and turned it on again. More tedium.

And the bugs that plague the NTT engine were annoying. One bug that kept on appearing unless i quit to main menu and reopened my save game was that after landing on a planet, one of the two characters i was with would shrink. Totally unfixable. 

On the topic of your second character, they're effectively useless in solo play. They just will REFUSE to help you in combat. And even if they do, they will miss entire saber swings or blaster shots. 

And if you decide to play this game in co-op, i hope your second player doesn't get too bored with basically not participating in most of the bigger sequences of the game. The final fight between Obi-Wan and Anakin in Revenge of the Sith? Player one gets to be Obi-wan, player two gets to stand there and watch as either C-3PO or R2-D2. Most of this game follows this ethos that goes against the second player having any fun. Which is a MAJOR step down in quality for a Lego game. A Tt Lego game at that.

After over 100 hours I have completed 100% of Lego Star Wars and have to say it is the best Lego game I have ever played.

What was good?

- Lots of planets to explore - 24 in total which are well filled
  with collectibles, quests or small challenges

- 45 levels, which offer a lot of variety

- Over 407 characters to explore the galaxy with.

- There are enough collectibles, like blue bricks,
  spaceships, characters, as always the minikits and the
  challenges that you can complete

- And of course the classic Lego humor which is as always throughout the game and often makes you smile.

- The graphics were excellent and let you experience the Lego world like never before.

What was bad?: 

The biggest problem Lego Star Wars has is that it is very repetitive in many places. Unfortunately, elements were often used more than once, especially in the collectibles and also for space battles, some quests and blue bricks.

Unfortunately, there are also some small bugs in the levels. For example, sometimes you can not complete some challenges or the level simply does not go on because certain cut scenes are not triggered.

Conclusion:

In the end I can say that Lego Star Wars The Skywalker Saga is a game that convinced me and can offer a lot of fun if you are interested in Lego or Star Wars games. I bought it at release, played the main story once and now set out to complete it to 100% and can say it was worth every penny for me. If you are not sure if you should buy it then maybe wait until it is reduced and give it a chance.

Overall I would give the game a rating of 8.5/10.

I played many of the Lego Games in the past, and even thou they were mostly the same, beside the settings, I always had a good time with them.
But they definitely needed an overhaul, and thankfully with this Game, they finally got it!     
                  
[u][b]Story[/b][/u]
Lego Star Wars The Skywalker Saga includes the Story of all 9 Movies in a compressed way. The cutscenes are cut down to the very basic information’s of the Story, which isn’t a bad thing directly, since the Lego games were never meant for long drawn out cutscenes. It can be hard to follow what’s going on thou in case you haven’t seen the Movies. Over the course of the Story, you visit all Iconic locations from the franchise like you would expect. 
You can choose to either begin the game at Episode 1, 4 or 7, depending on the order you want to experience them.      
          
[u][b]Gameplay[/b][/u]       
The gameplay is mostly the same as in the old games, destroy everything and loot studs! The game isn’t too hard and you don’t lose to much in case you die, its designed to be a relaxing, enjoyable experience and they definitely succeed with that. 
But thankfully, they did improve the game systems. The 380 Characters you can unlock are sorted into different categories like Jedi, Hero, Scavenger, Bounty Hunter, Droid etc. Each category has different skills you can invest into which can be upgraded in 3 Tiers each on top. You get skill points by collecting Special Bricks in each level, which are rewarded for different goals and challenges.
The combat system also got a general overhaul and is now more versatile compared to the old games.   
Beside that you can also collect Mini-kits, Vehicles and of course, new Characters. The levels feel bigger to me like in the old games and more open ended. Each is filled with a ton of Stuff to do, if you enjoy collecting Items and upgrades, you will find your happiness here. And like in the old games, the levels are designed in a way, that not everything can be looted the first time you visit a location. Some items need talents or Characters you will only obtain later to reach. 
        
[u][b]Graphic and Audio[/b][/u]       
The Graphic is a lovely mix of detailed Lego Models and Bricks/Structures and a more real general atheistic of the environments, which works out flawlessly in my eyes. 
The Audio is really good, it sounds like you would Star Wars expect to sound.   
                   
[u][b]Final Thoughts[/b][/u]    
If you enjoyed the old Lego games, you will immediately feel at home in the Skywalker Saga, all the new features, and a game that can be enjoyed solo or in coop with a friend, with the good Lego Humor on top guarantees a good time. 
If you are new to the Series and/or just found the game because you are a Star Wars fan and you are on the lookout for a relaxing game that can keep you busy for hours, or just for a while after a long day, I can fully recommend Lego Star Wars The Skywalker Saga to you as well!

100%'d the game so I've done every scripted thing you can do and what can I say about this.

Well for fans who wanted a LEGO Star Wars game as good as TCS since it came out, this is the answer you're looking for. It's humor and zany cutscenes have devolved since the older games, but the tradeoff is a complete rework including redone levels, an excellent combat system and an expansive galaxy that has a decently immersive effect.

First, the Story: The story does a more accurate job of retelling the saga with tons of decent voiceacting (you can turn off voice acting with mumble mode to have an older LEGO experience. I will say though, mumble mode isn't single mumbles, they mumble out entire sentences, so it feels a little weird), the cutscenes work with or without voiceacting which is a surreal dynamic experience that the devs get my kudos on, but the levels themselves are really short and kind've disappointing. They introduce "level challenges", there are 3 in every level and they're alternative ways of going about each one. They're fun in general, but if you're trying to 100% they can be a nightmare sometimes. Minikits have been reduced from 10 to 5 per level, which was debatably my favorite part about replaying a level. Overall, cutscene and immersion-wise, the levels are fun to play and have the same great puzzle-solving they've always had, replayability is quite low though.

First-Time through 9/10
Free-Play 100% 6/10 (basically, thank god they're short)

Now Galaxy-Mode was easily the most fun I've had through the whole experience. Instead of collecting gold bricks to a grand total of 250, (using the Marvel Avengers game as the mold here since it's the last one I 100%'d, god it sucked), there are 1,160 bricks, (known as "kyber bricks") that are collectable through completing level challenges, collecting minikits, getting "true jedi" on each level, doing side quests among 33 planets, destroying kyber comets, smuggling, doing bounty hunts, and puzzles on each and every planet. It was a ton of fun to mark each planet off the list as I collected each planets' worth. Some quests can only be done if you've progressed through the story up until that point, or until you've done other side quests. Personally, I recommend playing the base game all the way through 4-6, 1-3, 7-9, THEN doing galaxy-mode, so there will be less holdups. In advance, there was only 1 planet that gave me trouble and it was Endor, my guess is, the fire VFX would keep spawning as you loaded new areas, and it wouldn't unload areas you're not in anymore so the constant fire VFX made it a laggy shitshow. (However, entering a village hut loading zone, then exiting refreshed the lag, which led me to believe it was fire VFX that wouldn't unload.) Other than that, the quests and puzzles are really fun to complete.

9/10, it is the after-story experience you want.

I'll wrap it up here with the UI, combat/upgrade system, and the red bricks rework.
So the UI for the most part is pretty straightforward, might take a bit of learning but once you have it down, it all makes sense, stuff goes where it should go, changing characters is a bit messy and if you have OCD about how you want your free-play characters organized, that might be a huge problem because thats the only place where the UI falters heavily. Once you play, you'll figure out what I mean.

The combat system is EXTREMELY intricate, you have a third person firing mode with guns and saber-throwing. There's also cover you can hide behind (and rebuild if it gets destroyed) and shoot from if you want to play that way. The biggest highlight though is the melee combat system. You initiate combat with a standard attack which can then go into changeups like heavy attacks, uppercut moves, and spike moves, depending on which corresponding button you press. These changeups become extremely prevalent in the lightsaber boss duels which make you feel like you control how the corresponding movie-scene flows.

The red brick rework has been made easier to manage and deal with, you don't collect red bricks, instead you collect "Data cards" (1 per particular planet) in galaxy mode. They aren't specific to certain extras, you get the data card and choose which extra you want. (I recommend not buying anything until you get your first data card and do the stud multiplier route, things are hella expensive this time around so I'd say focus on getting all multipliers before you buy anything else) That being said "Stud magnet" and "Fast build" aren't extras anymore, they're "Upgrades"

The upgrade system integrates things like collecting studs, building faster, sprinting quicker, having more health, doing more damage, etc. which is where kyber bricks come in, as they are used as it's currency, plus an additional stud fee. (Now this is the exception to my advice about "not buying anything", buy upgrades when you can) There are core upgrades and class upgrades for specific character types, (Jedi, Hero, Bounty Hunter, Scoundrel, Scavenger, Villain, Dark Side, Astromech Droids, and Protocol Droids.) all of which have their own abilities and uses.

All of these features really make the experience flow a lot smoother and are a perfect 10/10 for me.



TL;DR: buy the game if you've been wanting a decent Lego Star Wars game, things are different for the better, mumble mode is there, and if you get deluxe, you get classic character packs (if nostalgia is your thing) among other misc. character packs. red bricks have been changed into a more easily flowing system, and the combat = good.

Big word of advice: once you're in galaxy mode, buy the rumor for the character "Grummgar", complete all the missions to get him and you get to run really fucking fast around some of these bigger planets to complete your side quests.

The Skywalker Saga feels too overambitious. Each movie only has 4 levels and they don't really feel as fleshed out as other Lego games. The plots for each movie are super abridged to accommodate for the short length of the campaign, neutering the story in favour of most of the plot taking place in the open world. About 60-70% of the story takes place in the open world, not in levels. Most of the 'gameplay' in the open world is walking through empty locations following objective markers to get to the next plot point, and that also suffers from a lot of backtracking and time wasting. The game is bloated and padded to hell and back to hide how little variation there is in the game.

The new additions to the game such as the enhanced combat feel unnecessary with how bland the level design is. Most enemies barely pose a threat to you, and that's not even considering the fact that death is pointless in Lego games as you instantly respawn with a few less studs.

Despite how this is meant to be a love letter to classic Lego games like The Complete Saga, they still don't capture the spirit of the originals since most of the cutscenes are just 1-1 recreations of their respective movie scenes but with Lego Minifigures, whereas fans of Complete saga enjoy it for the non-spoken slapstick comedy storytelling. They added the "mumble mode" extra but that doesn't address the root problem as the cutscenes are still 80% dialogue but the characters are just gagged now and make noises instead.

The game's development was plagued with tight work schedules and crunch culture, leading to a lot of scrapped content and the game being a buggy mess on launch, which it still is as the game barely got any bugfix patches in favour of adding several waves of DLC characters that aren't even voice acted, instead resorting to generic grunting noises.

Excellent AAA Ubisoft tier Open World Star Wars Game. Hits every nail on the head in that regard. But it fails to actually be a good Lego game comparable to the original classics it's trying to so hard to harken back to.

One of the most expansive lego games by far, before batman legacy of the dark knight comes out. It features levels adapting all nine main Star wars movies, with dlc covering spin-offs (don't get the dlc they are not worth it), it also features a lot of exploration and collectibles throughout the planets that feature in the movies as well as space it self, where you can fly spaceships, engage in combat and also board, take over and explore capital ships of all main factions.

I want to make the point that this game is not LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga. I know people wanted it to be, but it isn’t. The mechanics are different, the levels are different, the style is different, everything is different except for the story. There have been a lot of complaints about the level design being “too easy” or the levels are too short. Again, I want to point out that LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga came out 15 years ago and LEGO and Travelers Tales have changed their format, level design, and overall gameplay a few times over since then. I personally did not want a “remastered” game, I wanted a new game, one that would change the formula of LEGO games. I would say that this game definitely does that. To be clear, at the writing of this review, I have completed 6 of the 9 films on story mode alone (1,2,3,4,5,7).

Looking to the complaint of the short levels, I will agree, the levels are significantly shorter in this game than in the past. That does not mean, however, that there is less content. In addition, I think the voice actors do a great job of summarizing the Star Wars story with letting direct quotes and general set pieces direct the story. The one thing that seems to be more interesting about this game is that the open world is very integrated into the story. You have to go from one mission to the other (for the most part) by traveling to the planets yourself, or the different areas of said planets. The story definitely feels shorter, but I would say it reminds me of a “spark notes” version of Star Wars, especially with the voice acting in the game adding depth to the story. The mumble mode is a fun nostalgic call back to the old games, but in my unpopular opinion, it does not work for this game. The reason why it worked in the old games was because the characters mouths don’t move, but they are fully voice acted with detailed mouth movement. The Clone Wars voice actors sound phenomenal in the prequel trilogy and would highly recommend playing through with mumble mode off. Of course, I will play some stuff with mumble mode on for funs sake.

For those worried about trekking over everywhere to get to missions, there is a designated area in the menu to play just the missions again once it has been played through on story mode. This game still has a lot of unlockables, lots of upgrading, and plenty of time to spend hanging out in the Star Wars universe. The combat in this game is really new and exciting with “combos” being implemented as well as interesting mechanics with both lightsabers and blasters.

Overall, I would say this game is an exciting, fun, new aspect of not only the Star Wars franchise, but also LEGO games in general.

My first ever Lego game was actually the LEGO Star Wars Complete Trilogy. I remember playing that game for hours and hours unending, my family were lucky if they'd even got the chance to go to the computer before I did, this was back when most homes had only one computer. Now years later, playing this game made me feel exactly how I felt all those years ago.

This review is based on 100% completion and 62 hours of gameplay.

[h1][b]Recommendation:[/b][/h1]
Would I recommend this game? I would – as a game on its own, it’s fine, and it’s especially suitable for children. However, when I look at it specifically as a [i]LEGO Star Wars[/i] game and compare it to the earlier titles, I don’t think it stacks up very well.

I enjoyed my time far more with the older LEGO games, like [i]LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga[/i] or [i]LEGO Star Wars III: The Clone Wars (both on Xbox)[/i]. To me, this game feels over-engineered. It’s like they tried to cram in as much content and as many systems as possible, and that ended up having more of a negative effect than a positive one – at least for me. It’s a good example of why more isn’t always better. The older games felt tighter, simpler, and more polished overall.

Visually, the game is mostly very well done. The graphics are crisp, vibrant, and pleasant to look at, and they’ve clearly been brought up to modern standards. That said, the UI and menus are genuinely awful. Everything feels cluttered, claustrophobic, and annoying to navigate – especially on keyboard and mouse. It’s just not well optimised for PC, so I ended up playing entirely on controller, which at least felt better. Even then, for a kids’ game, there’s far too much going on in the menus. It feels bloated and overwhelming, especially in how everything interacts with everything else.

The sound design and voice acting are fine and well produced, but this is where the game really loses part of its identity for me. This entry adds full voice acting and dialogue, whereas the older LEGO games didn’t have it. While the voice lines themselves are done well, their inclusion takes away a big part of what made LEGO games feel like LEGO games. Yes, I know you can turn the voices off and enable the mumbling, but it’s not the same – the game was clearly designed around voiced dialogue.

The older LEGO games told their stories almost entirely through actions and visual gags, which conveyed more than enough and made you feel more immersed. [i]“Actions speak louder than words”[/i] really applied there. In this game, the story is largely told to you instead. There are still funny moments and typical LEGO humour throughout, but for me, the impact just isn’t the same. It’s all fine and competently done – I just think this is another part of the LEGO identity that’s been lost here.

Narratively, it’s okay overall [i](it’s Star Wars, after all)[/i], but because they’ve crammed in so much filler and fluff, the experience ends up feeling worse than previous LEGO Star Wars games. Everything up to Episode VI felt rushed to me, especially having already played those stories in earlier titles. Then when it gets to Episodes VII–IX, the pacing slows right down and becomes a complete slog. Personally, I think they should have stopped at [i]Return of the Jedi[/i]. Including that new sequel trilogy just drags the whole experience down, and getting through it was genuinely painful.

Gameplay and mechanics are also very hit and miss. I expect LEGO games to be easy, but this takes it to another level. I found the game mind-numbingly easy during both the main story and freeplay. There was zero challenge – combat and puzzles are incredibly basic – and I found myself taking frequent breaks simply because it was putting me to sleep.

There are also a lot of extra mechanics piled on top of each other, which adds to the feeling of overload. The camera can be really annoying and disorientating in certain sections, and the space combat is, in my opinion, the worst it’s ever been in a LEGO game. Flying feels sluggish and awkward, and during combat encounters you’re often better off just sitting still and shooting rather than actually manoeuvring. It constantly slows the game down for no real reason. Again, if I think about this purely as a kids’ game, it’s fine – but these issues do drag it down.

Performance on PC was mostly okay, but even on a fairly decent rig this game ran surprisingly hot. If you don’t have at least a mid-range PC, it might be worth holding off.

Overall, the game is fine for kids, but as a LEGO Star Wars title, I find it lacking compared to earlier entries. I wouldn’t recommend this at full price. It’s an older game now and regularly goes on sale, so I’d only suggest picking it up at a good discount.

[h1][b]Achievements:[/b][/h1]
[i][b]When it comes to achievements, there’s one big disclaimer I want to make clear straight away: there is an absurd amount of collectables and side missions required for 100%.[/b][/i]

This game is a massive grind. You’ll need at least two playthroughs – one story playthrough and then one freeplay. On top of that, you’ll need to freeplay the entire galaxy to mop up collectables and side missions, which takes a lot of time.

To give you a rough idea of the time investment: my initial story run took around 20 hours [i](including about 5 hours I had to replay due to a save error)[/i]. Completing all collectables and side missions in free play took me another 32.9 hours alone, even while rushing and skipping dialogue where possible. The free-play story cleanup run took a further 9 hours to finish off remaining collectables and challenges. Be prepared to sink a serious amount of time into this.

You don’t strictly need a guide, as the game has a decent tracking tab that shows what you’re missing. That said, because this is an older game, there are plenty of guides available if you need them. [b][i][url= https://www.youtube.com/@QuickBrickGames] Quick Brick Games [/url][/i][/b] on YouTube is a great option if you want to save time.

At the end of the day, the main thing to understand with this game is just how much busywork there is. You’re looking at well over 1,000 collectables and more than 100 side missions. If you’re going for 100%, lock in, put a film or podcast on in the background, and be ready for a long grind.

[H1]LEGO Star Wars: The Skywalker Saga — More Galaxy, Less LEGO Magic[/h1]

[b]Honestly? I'll take The Complete Saga over this any day of the year. [/b]

I went into this game cautiously optimistic. Hearing that it had a revamped aiming and shooting system, reworked mechanics, and a whole new approach to LEGO Star Wars gameplay sounded promising! I was genuinely looking forward to seeing how the formula had evolved since LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga and LEGO Star Wars III: The Clone Wars.

Sadly, I ended up enjoying this game a lot less than I expected.

[b]My biggest problem? THE VOICE ACTING. AGAIN. [/b]

I know fully voiced LEGO games have been around for years now, but that doesn't mean I'm ever going to stop missing the old style.

The genius of classic LEGO humor was that the characters didn't need dialogue. They communicated through exaggerated expressions, ridiculous physical comedy, and wonderfully stupid LEGO-related shenanigans. You could understand exactly what a character was feeling without a single spoken word, and somehow that made everything ten times funnier.

The silence was part of the charm. The expressions were the punchline. The animations did the storytelling.

And now? Characters just talk. And talk. And talk some more.

It makes the humor feel so much flatter to me. The personality that used to come through in those hilarious little nonverbal moments just doesn't hit the same way when everything is spelled out through dialogue.

I know some people love the voice acting, and fair enough! But for me, it takes away a huge part of what made the older LEGO games so special. I don't need LEGO characters explaining the joke when watching them silently do something incredibly stupid was already the joke. 

[b]And then there's the open world... or should I say, the open-world marathon. [/b]

I understand why the developers wanted to create huge, explorable planets. The worlds look fantastic, the character designs are more detailed, and everything feels much closer to the actual Star Wars universe than in the older games.

But bigger doesn't automatically mean better.

There is just SO MUCH TRAVERSAL. Running around enormous areas to reach the next objective gets tedious, and instead of feeling like an exciting adventure across the galaxy, it sometimes feels like I'm spending half my time commuting to the fun part.

Apparently, they learned the wrong lessons from Jedi: Fallen Order and Jedi: Survivor. 

I don't mind exploration when it feels rewarding, but here, the sheer amount of traveling often feels like padding rather than meaningful gameplay. I'd rather have tighter, more focused levels packed with creative set pieces, clever puzzles, and classic LEGO comedy than a massive map that makes me wish my character had a speeder with a skip-travel button.

[b]Yes, the game looks better. But does it FEEL better? Not to me. [/b]

I'd happily trade the prettier graphics, more elaborate worlds, and voiced dialogue for the old games' visual comedy, focused level design, and that unmistakable LEGO personality.

[b]The Skywalker Saga tries to do more, but somehow feels like less. [/b]

Maybe that's a bit harsh, and I can absolutely see why someone who prefers modern open-world games would enjoy it more than I did. But as someone who grew up loving the older LEGO Star Wars games, this just didn't scratch the same itch.

Give me The Complete Saga. Give me LEGO Star Wars III: The Clone Wars. Give me silent characters communicating exclusively through increasingly ridiculous facial expressions and slapstick comedy.

I miss that magic, and this game reminded me just how special it was.

[b]5/10[/b] The galaxy is bigger, the graphics are prettier, and the characters can talk... but I still want my old LEGO Star Wars back.

[h2]tl;dr[/h2]

massive, content-heavy LEGO Star Wars game with a fresh formula, but dragged down by a mediocre story mode and an absolutely soulless grind; full package simply not worth it

[h2]Overview[/h2]

LEGO Star Wars: The Skywalker Saga brings together all nine mainline Star Wars movies in one package, reinventing the classic LEGO gameplay. The game introduces a more modern third-person perspective, delves into third-person-shooter-territory, expands into semi-open hub worlds across multiple planets, and puts a strong emphasis on exploration, collectibles, and player freedom.

[h2]The Good Stuff[/h2]

There’s no denying the sheer amount of content. You get a wide range of planets to explore, each with its own little hubs, secrets, and activities. The game leans heavily into a semi-open-world structure, giving you a lot of freedom to roam around and discover things at your own pace. The updated formula works surprisingly well in parts. Moving away from the old static camera to a more modern third-person perspective gives the gameplay a slightly fresher feel. The introduction of character classes is also a solid addition, making it clearer which abilities are tied to which characters and how to approach certain obstacles.

LEGO humor still does its job. It’s light, charming, and consistently manages to get a grin out of me, even if the rest of the experience starts to drag. Some boss fights are also worth mentioning. While inconsistent overall, the better ones feel like a simplified introduction to mechanics you’d find in more complex games, which makes them a nice entry point for younger players.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3671883846
[h2]The Sorta-Kinda-Grinds-My-Gears-Stuff[/h2]

The story mode is easily the weakest part. It often feels like a walking simulator with short, mediocre levels sprinkled in between. The game is clearly designed around exploration, which is fine, but if you try to push through the story (knowing you’ll have to replay everything in free mode anyway), it becomes a slog of constant running from point A to B. Boss fights are hit or miss. Some are creative and fun, others are just annoyingly bad.

The whole “hundreds of characters” selling point is, as usual, mostly meaningless. You end up using the same handful of characters or classes anyway, making the massive roster feel more like marketing fluff than actual gameplay depth.

Technical issues don’t help either. Crashes and bugs occur, and considering how the game is structured into many smaller areas instead of a few large ones, the loading times feel surprisingly long. The UI is another weak point. It feels bloated, cluttered, and unintuitive, making navigation more tedious than it should be.

[h2]The Atrociously-Bad Stuff[/h2]

The grind.

This is where the game completely falls apart. With around 1200 bricks, hundreds of collectibles, and an overwhelming amount of side activities, completion turns into pure busywork. It’s not challenging, it’s not engaging, it’s just exhausting. It feels like Ubisoft on steroids, lacking any inspiration.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3654797537
[h2]Achievement-Hunter-Things[/h2]

Full completion is not difficult, just incredibly time-consuming. It essentially boils down to “do everything,” and there’s a lot of everything. I straight up abandoned any completionist aspirations. The grind simply wasn’t enjoyable and my body legitimately rebelled against the idea of moving on. The riddles and side activities don’t add meaningful variety, they just stretch the playtime. If you’re going for 100%, be prepared for a long, repetitive cleanup phase with very little payoff. 

[h2]Conclusion[/h2]

LEGO Star Wars: The Skywalker Saga is a strange one. On the surface, it’s exactly what it promises: a massive LEGO Star Wars experience with tons of content, freedom, and a modernized formula. But the more you play, the more it starts to feel hollow. The story mode lacks substance, the open-world design turns into busywork, and the grind for completion is genuinely exhausting. Compared to older titles like LEGO The Lord of the Rings or LEGO The Hobbit, which could get tedious but still remained fun, this one never reaches that level of enjoyment. Not even remotely. 

If you just want a casual LEGO Star Wars experience, or if you just want one game to sink a lot of time into, it is fine, I guess. Preferably get it during a sale, it isn't really expensive anymore. But as a full package? Not really worth it.

This is a difficult game to review, as it occupies a very odd space where it is simultaneously a children's game and a game for fans who played the original LEGO Star Wars games as kids. Your expectation coming into the game is honestly what decides if you love it or hate it.

The game does not have much depth. There is a huge abundance of content if you go by the numbers. Tons of characters to play as, tons of ships to fly, stuff to break, and places to go. There's just not much to it beyond that; nearly all the puzzles are very simple, and all of the characters in a class play almost identically aside from animations and voice lines.

Most severely though, is that the combat is mind-numbingly simple and free of all challenge. You will need to go out of your way to be killed by any of the bosses, let alone normal enemies. The combat does have a lot of flair, you can string together some pretty neat combos that look super cool, but there's not any advantage to this over just spamming one of the attack buttons.
The pacing of the episodes also leaves a lot to be desired. Each episode has a couple open worlds you get thrown into, and right away you're strung along with a couple "go here, watch this cutscene"-type objectives and are then dumped into a level that, most likely, will drag on long after you stopped having fun. Repeat ad nauseam.

Not all is bad, though. As stated there are an insane number of characters and ships to use, and a good number of the cutscenes are pretty charming. There are some puzzles that are actually engaging and require a decent amount of critical thinking or creative solutions. Ultimately the game doesn't utilize these very often, and you can generally expect monotonous puzzles that have the same song and dance that you've been through 50 times.

There is also not much reward for your efforts; getting Kyber Bricks exist to make your completion number go up and to buy skills for your character. There a few indispensable skills such as stud magnet, and running speed, but the others have little to no impact on the gameplay. I promise you won't need extra health bars or even any class-specific skills, the game is trivial enough without them.

Ultimately I feel I need to thumbs down this game. Unless you are buying this for your child, or you are a child, there is virtually nothing here that will keep you entertained for very long.
It is a sin to put Rey on the top of the main menu of a game about the "Skywalker Saga". This game is enjoyable regardless.

Fantastic game! It's 100% clear to me that TT Games has made this with the old games in mind; not as a replacement, but as a successor, a game that kindly respects them rather than ignorantly bypassing them. (It even uses the original minikit collection sound as it's build complete sound! I have too many hours on The Original Trilogy and Complete Saga to ever forget that satisfying bit of audio.)

The game has taken to a completely different set of levels. Instead of raiding the Jedi Temple in Episode 3, you'll be fighting Sidious in the senate chamber. Instead of fighting a bounty hunter mid-flight in the first level of Episode 2, you'll be exploring, trying to figure out what that dart thing really is.
Frankly, it's a much more immersive way of going about the story. In LGS (The Prequels), you'd finish fighting Grevious then immediately transition to running and fighting clones on Kashyyyk, with little to no story explanation; it was a bit of a mess. Don't get me wrong, the levels were fantastic (and specifically levels 1 and 6 of Episode 3 had some of the best design of many of them.)
Even in The Original Trilogy, you'd go from murdering Jabba the Hut to going around in speeders; the games seemed to be picking specific points to hit from the movies rather than retelling them, and that resulted in games that weren't all that immersive; games that really were a bit scrambled.

This game is different. While the levels may be short, they're very involved and combat-filled. And, when you finish a level, you don't teleport to the next level automatically, you're still within the relative area of where you finished it; you have to travel to the next level yourself (or stay where you are and get Kyber Bricks, a fantastic part of the game that I can't stop participating in), really showing off the fantastic galaxy TT has made. The more story you complete, the more planets you have (and you can go anywhere anytime!)

The game is a bit of a fabricated experience, though; it shows you what to do, and actively directs you towards that goal. You're always able to go your own direction, but you cannot 'untrack' the story mission, it is always tracked. You'll always have a tiny orange exclamation on your screen, nearly 24/7, adding to the odd smattering of UI elements the game's dropped on your screen. 

Of course, a fabricated experience isn't a bad thing; it's a kid's game, after all, meant for a very wide audience, not just 20-30 year old gamer nerds. The game does let you tune these to an extent (you can disable or enable consequence-free falling, for example, reducing stud loss to 0 when you fall into the void), but not everything can be turned off or skipped. For example, the game will give you a tutorial when it deems you should be shown it, locking your controls and forcing you to do what it's asking. You can't turn them off, either; just do what it's telling you to do. It's a little infuriating, to be honest.

That's all nitpicking, though. In it's entirety, this is a massive, beautiful game, with a ton of massive, beautiful environments, and a ton of massive, beautiful levels (that are short in a linear sense, but have so much exploration to them that more than makes up for it!)

I highly recommend this game, it IS worth the price. (For reference, I can count the times I've paid $60 for a game in the past 10 years on my left hand.)

[h1]Mostly Worth the Wait![/h1]

We've been waiting since 2019 for [i]LEGO Star Wars: The Skywalker Saga[/i], originally scheduled for spring of 2020, to be released.  The delay was not all due to the pandemic.

Was it worth waiting for?

Er, mostly. Storyline is the usual solid adaptation, but the collectathon/completionist partcontimues looonnnnggg afteward.


The game is organized into the nine movie episodes, plus a Galaxy Exploration for easy access to the hub worlds for Free Play.

Since each trilogy has its ardent fans (and detractors), the game makes the opening of the first movie of each (Ep I: The Phantom Menace, Ep IV: A New Hope, and Ep VII: The Force Awakens) available to you from the start, so you can go to your favorite trilogy first or save it for last.


The game engine has been rebuilt, but not reinvented.  Most of the gameplay will feel familiar to anyone who has played any other game in the TT Games LEGO franchise.

In solo or co-op play, players switch amongst at least two characters, using their various abilities to solve puzzles and advance through the levels.

Levels have a variety of segments.  Some are simple exploring.  The light saber duels are represented and involve lots of button mashing, often with breaks to chase the opponent and do more exploring.  There are some spaceship chases, and destroying enemy big ships.

New are the combos you can do in battles for extra power or for more money from defeated mooks.  These are not particularly needed, though, and just hitting X a dozen times works, too.

With all the shootouts in the franchise, the devs have provided some low cover that both sides can use.  I've never been into shooters, and mostly resorted to the Jedi.  It is slightly annoying to have my character slip into a "taking cover" pose when near the barriers that make up the cover.  The barriers are rebuildable, and the pieces become distractions with their "build me!" animation.


A brand new twist here are the Classes.  Characters in these games have always seemed to fall into various categories or classes, and here they are official.  

Classes here are Jedi (Luke, Obi-Wan, Yoda), Dark Side (Vader, the Emperor, Maul), Protocol Droids (C-3PO), Astromechs (R2-D2, BB-8), Bounty Hunters (the Fetts, Leia as Boussh), Scavengers (Rey), plus Heroes (Leia, Padme, soldiers for the good guys), and Villains (Empire and First Order officers and stormtroopers).  There's also an Extra category for characters that don't fit easily or can't be used well, such as some tiny droids.  As usual, the devs give you almost every character model they whipped up to use, even if the cutscene or level segment missed the cut.

All characters in a class have the same abilities, with no unique additions or combos.  On the one hand, this makes it easy to remember which character can do what.  On the other hand, it also prevents the devs from giving a character a unique ability (Think both hobbitty Baggins with the One Ring.)

The distribution of abilities is always a source of annoyance for fans of a property adapted into a LEGO game.  Someone somewhere is always scratching their heads over why a certain character was given (or not given) a particular ability.

For example, both Bounty Hunter Fetts have a jetpack, but cannot fly with them, even though both use them as bosses.  The Jedi and Dark Side share an odd one, using their light sabers to climb walls by sticking them in the wall and pulling it up.  And Heroes, Villains, and Astromechs all have their own terminals mainly to open stuff up.

On the other hand, one of the best abilities is given to the Protocol Droids.  Hub world NPCs speak several different languages.  Many characters know a few languages, but only the protocol droids, created specifically to help in diplomatic affairs, know ALL of them.

The Classes each get their own set of Upgrades, and there are ones for the whole game as well.  This not a min-max system, as you can jump in at almost anywhere and can accomplish most things without getting a single upgrade.  Rather, these are simply things that make the game a bit easier or faster, such as stronger hits, a greater health bar, more shielding for ships, or bypassing the repetitive minigames for Hero/Villain terminals.


The sheer size of the game world(s) gives you a daunting task if you are a completionist tackling the collectathon part of the game.

Seriously, the galaxy here is HUGE!  Almost a couple dozen planets to visit, some with a couple different areas to go to.  And some of the planetside areas are large in themselves, often beating the expansive Manhattan of the LEGO Marvel games.

The main thing to collect are the Kyber Bricks ([i]1200[/i] of them!), a reference to the kyber crystals that power light sabers and give them their color.  This is the game's version of what are normally Gold Bricks.

A chunk of them are awarded simply for completing the levels or accomplishing various things in the levels, such as for completing minikits (micro version of space ships in the game) or each of the three tiers of True Jedi money quotas.  (The partial credit is new and a nice touch; it's very difficult to reach the full amount in Story Mode.)

New this game are Challenges.  Get all three for a level and you earn a Kyber Brick.  Some are easy, such as simply rolling to shake a homing missile in the flight levels.

Some however, I found very difficult, such as: [spoiler]Dodging Jango Fett's missile attacks so you don't get hit once ... in a three-phase boss level ... in an asteroid belt.  Yeah.  Took me 10+ hours off and on to get.[/spoiler]

You have to either luck into completing the Challenges, buy the hint in the in-game menu, or just find the solution in an walkthrough.  The hints can be tricky to figure out.

The hub world collectibles include more bricks, character or vehicle access (you still have to pay to fully unlock them), and datacards.

There are the standard races, on land and in space.  In space, the races include Scramble Runs, in which you do not have to pass through the gates in a particular order.

In space, you can destroy a Kyber Comet for a few bricks, or be offered smuggling runs to another planet.  You can even take over a capital ship (the Dreadnoughts, Star Destroyers) by destroying its defenses and defeating its captain.

Hub world collectives include Datacards.  With one of these and enough money, you can unlock the Extras that in past games were earned with specific Red Bricks.  These include the traditional money multipliers and some stuff's just fun and silly, such as the Cantina Song on a loop, or light sabers looking like baguettes.

Both non-flight levels and hub worlds have maps.  The hubs even have indicators for various things, including useful NPCs who will tell you about collectibles.  Some just point you to the nearby brick, others send you offworld.  Recruitable characters ask you for a favor before they will let you use them.

Many missions will have you hopping from planet to planet.  There are also a couple "find all of us" missions, including hunting the mouse droids and finding a wookie tourist on every planet.

The game has a shooting (and light saber toss) FPS mode.  As I don't usually play FPS games, it took me a while to figure out the controls.  A tutorial game would have helped.  There are some aim assist toggles, though, and one tap sets the gun to continual fire.  However, there is a shooting gallery (to earn a vehicle) that the aim assist doesn't work/help with.

This is when I had my ragequit moment.  I had sunk a bit over 100 hours in the game ALREADY (including 10 or so on one particular level's challenge), well over the time on any other LEGO game, and still had about 30% left.  I had the satisfaction of completing the trilogy of trilogy levels, including everything in Free Play, but wasn't going get everything as I usually do in these games.  So, time to move on.

But it was still a fun ride for most of the way.
17 hour walking simulator stacked on top of a 100 hour collectathon. if you're a chimp like me who enjoys the dopamine hit of collecting worthless garbage, you'll love this game.

I don't think the game is bad, I think it's just not for me. I think if you're young, or have a child to play with, I'd say this is awesome. But I just don't care much for this. Despite what I write below, I do recommend this game, as it is a decent LEGO game, but there are just some things I couldn't get over. 

1. The Missions
missions felt WAY too short, often lasting like 5-10 minutes max. They removed a lot of puzzles compared to older games, and big movie moments are often in cutscenes, and not gameplay, which felt like a wasted opportunity. It lacks in design depth. 

2. Open World
Tons of planets, with big areas, but yet... empty? Many of the areas feel repetitive, with fetch quests and lacking any meaningful interaction. Like it's big, but not engaging, just get what u need done next planet moving on. 

3. Combat
They added a new over the shoulder FPS type combat system, which felt modern, but button mashy, it isn't challenging, and they made saber combat extremely simplified. Not that LEGO games are known for complex combat, but they could've done something with it. It just doesn't feel like a true action game..

4. Puzzles 
I am sorry but they just feel less creative. Followthe marker! Type objectives annoy me. I get it if there's a setting for it, but it's default and I just felt like there are less puzzles than previous installments. UI guides and waypoints were just way too simple. 

5. Humor
I'm old, I accept I'm biased, but I just really prefer silent comedy over this. The voice acting in theory is better, but the cheesy jokes, the overly forced humor, it felt bad. It's more of a retelling than a parody, instead of smirking or chuckling over the jokes, I just get a sense of "oh.."

5. Bugs
When it launched, it was bugsgalore. But they DID patch it. They did put effort into the game, and I can't hold it against them, but it was pretty bad at launch. I would say this just shows they did care to patch it, which I appreciate that. 

6. Characters
I'll be honest, a massive roster (a kids dream), but in reality, it's just like a slight cosmetic change. All the characters are too similar, lacking identity. If they somehow made more of them feel unique, I'd be onboard, but instead it just feels washed. 

7. Story
Again, with the missions being short, a lot of the important stuff in cutscenes, the story's pace felt rushed, condensing things quite a bit, feeling like important things were just a highlight, and not lived. 

Now bottom line, I'm still recommending it, I think kids will love it, which I have to realize, that's truly what LEGO games are about. I think despite my problems with it, I think there are people who just wanted a modern Complete Saga, something we've been waiting for for a long time. I couldn't recommend this game enough with your child, or maybe a friend who just wants to chill and play a silly little game. This game does go on sale for 10 dollars, which is DEFINITELY worth it. So if you want to just create a memory with a youngster, go for it!

Hear me out: I would actually recommend this game if it’s on sale for under $15 and/or you only want to play through the 9 movies while enjoying the typical, great LEGO humor. But that’s pretty much it.
Before we come to all the negativity i also have some positive things to say about the game.
-- The graphics are great compared to the old games.
-- The open world is filled with stuff to immerse in the world, collect or interact with stuff. they did a great job filling it so it doesnt feel empty at any point.
-- the new combo based combat system is a massive upgrade over the old button mashing, and new features like the different terminals are genuinely cool at first.
I do NOT recommend this game to anyone going for 100% completion or looking for a nostalgia trip based on The Complete Saga or LEGO Star Wars III: The Clone Wars. The Skywalker Saga is literally worse in almost every single way compared to the classics, aside from graphics and the inclusion of the sequel trilogy.
Here are the main negative points, which are simply too much for a $50 game:
1. Level Design,
-- Short & Fragmented: About 95% of the story levels are tiny 2–3 minute segments flooded with aircraft missions or boss fights. Both are cool in moderation, but not in this insane amount.
-- Chapter 1 Breakdown: It is literally: Aircraft -> Aircraft -> Boss Fight -> Mini-Level -> Aircraft. Where is the actual normal gameplay? (in my opinion the aircraft and bossfight lvls are a great addition to the game, but they are just way too much compared to the amount of "normal" lvls like back then in the complete saga)
-- The Level Split: Out of the 45 story levels, there are 13 aircraft missions, 15 boss fights, and only 17 "normal" levels (which are still super short.(i hope i didnt misscount anything lol))
2. Open World: Quantity Over Quality,
-- Repetitive Grind: Exploring 24 planets sounds awesome, but collecting ~1,000 Kyber Bricks in the open world gets insanely boring after Planet 3. It’s the exact same 4-5 mechanics over and over and over again.
-- Pointless Rewards: All those bricks just go into class upgrades that barely impact gameplay.
-- Annoying Space Encounters: Smuggling missions tear you out of hyperspace up to 3 times per trip just to destroy 8–12 weak enemy ships. A cool gimmick at first, but incredibly tedious very quickly.
3. Disappointing Upgrades & Extras,
-- Useless Class Upgrades: Out of 36 class upgrades, around 22 feel completely pointless and don't change how you play at all. (not including the general upgrades which are all really good)
-- Missing Quality-of-Life: Besides Stud Multipliers and the Universal Translator, the Datacard extras are mostly just visual jokes (Baguette lightsabers, Gonk NPCs or Retro Look).
-- Where are the Real Cheats? Classics like Invincibility are missing. Worst of all: where is an "Auto-Hack" extra? Doing the exact same terminal mini games hundreds of times calls for an endgame upgrade to skip the mini-game and replace it with a quick 1-2 second animation.
4. Wasted Potential & Missing Content,
-- No "Buy All" Button: With 380 characters and 69 ships, forcing players to buy every single item individually is a huge QoL oversight.
-- Zero Bonus Levels: This is my personal biggest missed opportunity. I LOVED the bonus levels back in The Complete Saga or Clone Wars 3. Why isn't there a single one? Why not add one bonus level per chapter, or special planet levels—like a Mandalorian-inspired level for Tatooine, a Clone Wars 3 PvP mode for Geonosis, or a Tower Defense mode after 100%-ing Chapter 1? Imagine the Battle of Naboo from a top-down view, building Gungan catapults, shields, and deploying troops against waves of droids. I missed stuff like that so much.
5. Bugs & Broken Triggers,
-- I had to restart my game multiple times because collectibles for missions failed to register.
-- Capital ships spawned half outside the map boundaries, making them impossible to board or destroy.
-- Level challenges regularly bugged out, requiring 3+ identical playthroughs before the game finally awarded the Kyber Brick.

Conclusion:
It is a great game if you buy it on sale for under $15 just to enjoy the 9 movies with the classic LEGO humor. But if you are here to enjoy the story AND grind it to 100% like I did, this game is just soul-crushing. All the issues above turn the endgame into a massive chore. I am relieved to finally have my 100%, but I will never ever touch this game again.

And I'm saying this as someone who played The Complete Saga a dozen times, enjoying every single 100% playthrough from start to finish. The Skywalker Saga completely failed my expectations and is simply not worth $50. If this game was $20, I wouldn't complain as much but for $50, it's just a huge disappointment. Cannot recommend.

The game is beautiful. The gameplay is fun and kind of mindless, the missions are fun and see all these worlds looking how they do, it really is a feast for the eyes. Hats off to Tt Games. They've nailed the world.

The main gripe is the grind. If you want to hit 100%, prepare yourself to collect 1200, yes one thousand two hundred Kyber bricks. The missions and challenges are very easy to complete and there is no sense of accomplishment. Just grind. These missions are their most tedious where, to get one kyber brick, you must travel to 3 other planets and do 3 missions, just for one brick on a wholly different planet. It is unnecessary bloat. To quote Count Dooku "Surely you can do better!"

If you aren't bothered about 100% - grab this game. it is wonderful.

If you want 100% and you have a job.... good luck finding the time. I am 780 bricks in and I hopped on to play and continue my grind today, only to be immediately bored after collecting 3.

I will recommend it because I have decided to not 100% this game (yet) and for what I have played in terms of the non bloat content, it is lovely.

The most fun lego game ever, there's so much content, so much nostalgia it's insane, so many worlds you can explore, so much you can do. Really the biggest flaw is no character customization, but that's really it. If your looking for a fun star wars game and don't mind the lego humor this is for you, if you love lego and star wars again, this game is for you.

This game feels like a husk of a Lego game: The developers went with a very formulaic design instead of trying to make the game actual fun:
* Most "missions" involve walking from A to B, talking a bit, sometimes a cut scene, and being dumped back in the hub area, just to walk to the next mission. There is usually one 5-10 minute mission per 1h hub area.
* Lots of loading time... made worse by the mission  design which loads a new level for 30s of walking.
* Many missions are uninspired: You are not doing anything interesting, varied, ...
* Some missions were clearly not tested / designed in co-op, with the 2nd player not being able to do anything for some time
* Hub areas are littered with collectibles that require little to no thought to collect.... just enduring the tedium. less than 5% of the tasks actually require some though. With more than 1400 things to collect it is all quantity, no quality.
* Inconsistent UI/controls, and in general lack of polish and streamlining

Altogether it feels like they were just doing the game by-the-numbers, instead of iterating the design, and much to the detriment of fun missions, and puzzles. It's a shame, but it seems the developer do not really know what made some of the older ones fun (Lego Lord of the Rings is still one of my favourite)

LEGO Star Wars: The Skywalker Saga is the latest in the long running line of licensed LEGO games from Traveller's Tales. It was also one of the most heavily anticipated games in the entire TT LEGO series. And why is that? Well, for 2 reasons... 1, the trailer looked amazing. But also because it was one of the titles that spent the most time in development and promised the most new features and changes to the series. If you look back at the long line of games you'd see we got a new LEGO title pretty much annually. In some years we even got as many as 2 or 3 new LEGO titles. Basically Traveller's Tales was pumping these out like clockwork. And then after 2019, after the release of The LEGO Movie 2 Videogame, nothing. We got our first glimpse in 2020, but it would not be for another 2 years until the game finally released. A little over 3 years between games. Yes, the anticipation for this one was as strong as the force. But was it really worth the wait? 

Skywalker Saga takes the formula of past LEGO games and makes a bold choice to switch things up, which results in a few steps forward, but also a few steps back. Where the game really shines would be in 3 key areas: Action, exploration and unlockables. But where it suffers mostly would be in the overall flow of the main game. 

The game is comprised of 45 stages spanning all 9 movies with 5 stages per movie. The stages are tied together by segments that will have you go through some of the free roam areas, but in general they are rather short. Most of the playtime will be spent revisiting stages to unlock things you could not access before with new characters in free play mode. It's a bit of a downer when compared to previous LEGO games, and this is primarily due to the fact that levels are not padded with puzzles but rather focus more on action segments with minimal puzzles, which is a 180 turn compared to previous titles. While the game does do a good job capturing many key moments from the movies, there are also a lot of key scenes at the same time that fans will notice are missing, or heavily compressed into short segments in cutscenes. While it's not unusual for LEGO games to rush through story pieces taken from movies, it is still a major bummer since we waited this long. 

Luckily the game makes up for some of this in other areas. For starers revisiting some stages is a blast. While some are going to be short no matter what, others do feel a tad bigger when revisiting to unlock things. Also the free roaming areas for the most part are massive with tons of side quests and lots of things to unlocks. You'll spend a lot of time hunting down these new things called kyber crystals, which are essentially the replacement for gold bricks. In past lego games gold bricks did not hold much merit. Some games allowed you to accept new quests if you got so many gold bricks, but that was pretty much it. Kyber crystals on the other hand can be used for currency to unlock new abilities or enhance character classes. And there are a ton of these to collect also, with over 1,000 of them scattered across the entire galaxy. 

Combat is also another major improvement over past LEGO games. In previous titles combat was simple, and pretty much a straight up button masher. That's not to say this one is not also a button masher. It still can be. But there is also a bit of strategy to be found here as you can pull off combos now. Sometimes enemies will even block your attacks if you mash the same button over and over, forcing you to press other attack buttons. It's a small change, but its still a very welcome one that takes away from the tedium of pressing the same attack buttons over and over. Ranged combat has also been overhauled, as you can freely aim in any direction now like a traditional over the shoulder 3rd person shooter. Some enemies will even have reactions depending on which body part you hit. Like shooting at their legs may make them fall over, or shooting the helmets of stormstroopers will actually make them fly off revealing the lego heads underneath for a followup headshot resulting in an instant kill. You can even sneak up on enemies for stealth kills. Hell, there's even a counter button, though I did not see much opportunity to use it as the LEGO characters you play as already seem kind of overpowered as usual not giving you many opportunities to need to use the counters. But when you do get an opportunity the counter will result in a special move reminiscent of some of the flashy spectacular special moves you'd see in some of the past lego games. Some of them very good for crowd control too. Needless to say, the combat changes overall are a very welcome addition to Skywalker Saga.

Aerial and space combat is also a welcome change. In past games that featured this you usually had 2 types of aerial and space combat: On rails or tilted top down. Now there are still a few on rails segments here, but they have ditched the tilted top down space combat for full control of your spaceships, meaning you can get into  some full 3D dogfight action for once! And it's a blast when you are in these stages. You'll be weaving in and out tie fighters with your X-Wing, Millennium Falcon or whatever ship you have access to while taking down the enemies or shooting at cannons, satellite dishes or other objects on massive space stations or dreadnoughts or other massive spacecraft. Sadly this type of combat is limited to certain stages, and the space sections you'll find while exploring the galaxy are just that... space. It would have been nice to see more action in the free roaming space sections. 

Visually Skywalker Saga looks phenomenal. The name of the game is anything but realism, and instead your characters are all comprised the typical LEGO bricks. I mean we are talking a LEGO game. But the mixture of solid animation and little details make it a visual treat. You'll find little visual nods like when you walk around Tatoonie seeing bits of sand getting stuck to your minifigs, or walking through the snowy tunnels of Hoth and seeing your bricks getting snow stuck to them. Cutscenes also have some wonderful animation that look like a proper CG movie. Very spectacular and a great treat to behold. And the overall look of the worlds is also eye candy on the LEGO scale. Like many past LEGO games, it is a mix of bricks and more realistic looking set pieces also. Typically if it is made of bricks it can also be destroyed, so some areas can get completely wrecked leaving bricks scattered. Sadly the chaos does not last as bricks do disappear when destroyed after a short period. But all the same it is very satisfying breaking things down. 

Mostly the game runs great for me playing at 3440x1440 with an RTX 2080 Super playing on max settings. The overall stability of the game is far from perfect however  as there are still some bugs to be ironed out. I have had the game crash to desktop on me a total of 4 times in the 25+ hours I have played so far. 2 of the crashes while revisiting the General Grievous. There are also 2 areas which also are prone to massive frame drops even on high end machines as multiple people have reported (myself included). Those 2 areas being the Droid Factory Frenzy stage and the Ewok Village. Traveller's Tales is aware of some of these issues so now it is just a matter of how long before they are fixed. But when not encountering the 2 aforementioned sections the game runs extremely well for the most part. 

Pros:
Amazing changes to combat
Huge open world hubs
Tons of collectables
Aerial and space combat is extremely fun

Cons: 
Story skips or rushes through several key segments
Bugs still need to be ironed out
Open world space sections feel underwhelming

Overall, I think Skywalker Saga was indeed worth the wait. It might not be perfect, and some parts do feel rushed, but that aside I have had a blast so far playing the game.
